Absolutely Delightful Table-making in Python

Great Tables turns DataFrames into display tables: the kind of table you'd find in a report, a journal article or on a web page. Give a table a header and footer, group and label its rows and columns, format every kind of value, and style any part of it. Then, if you like, hand it to your readers to sort, filter and search in the browser.

[Get started](./user-guide/introduction.md) [See the examples](./examples/) [Browse the reference](./reference/index.md)

`$`` pip install great_tables`

### Build a table, one layer at a time

A table is made by chaining methods onto [GT()](./reference/GT.md#great_tables.GT), each adding a part of the table, a format or a style. Step through the layers of this one to see what each adds; the new lines of code are highlighted.

``` python
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, GTI, data, loc, md, nanoplot_options, style

regions = {
    "IN": "Asia", "CN": "Asia", "ID": "Asia", "PK": "Asia", "BD": "Asia",
    "US": "Americas", "BR": "Americas",
    "NG": "Africa",
}

# The eight most populous countries of 2022, with their populations in 1960 and 2022, and
# (in millions) every five years between
countries = (
    data.pl.countrypops
    .filter(pl.col("country_code_2").is_in(list(regions)))
    .sort("year")
    .group_by("country_code_2", "country_name", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(
        pop_1960=pl.col("population").first(),
        pop_2022=pl.col("population").last(),
        trend=(pl.col("population") / 1e6).round(1).filter(pl.col("year") % 5 == 0),
    )
    .with_columns(
        region=pl.col("country_code_2").replace_strict(regions),
        change=pl.col("pop_2022") / pl.col("pop_1960") - 1,
    )
    .sort("pop_2022", descending=True)
    .select("country_code_2", "country_name", "region", "pop_1960", "pop_2022", "change", "trend")
)
```

Data

It starts with a DataFrame: here, the eight most populous countries, from [data.countrypops](./reference/data.countrypops.md#great_tables.data.countrypops). [GT()](./reference/GT.md#great_tables.GT) takes Polars, Pandas and PyArrow tables as they are.

Structure

Add a title, group the rows by region, put a spanner over the population columns, label the columns and cite the source.

``` python
(
    GT(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960-2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
)
```

Format

Turn country codes into flags and populations into millions and billions, show the change as a percentage, and draw each list of populations as a small plot.

``` python
(
    GT(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960-2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
    .fmt_flag(columns="country_code_2")
    .fmt_number(columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"], compact=True, n_sigfig=3)
    .fmt_percent(columns="change", decimals=0, force_sign=True)
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", options=nanoplot_options(show_data_points=False))
    .text_replace("United States", "USA", locations=loc.body(columns="country_name"))
)
```

Style

Color each change by its size, set the countries and regions in bold, add a footnote and set the header to the left.

``` python
(
    GT(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960-2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
    .fmt_flag(columns="country_code_2")
    .fmt_number(columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"], compact=True, n_sigfig=3)
    .fmt_percent(columns="change", decimals=0, force_sign=True)
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", options=nanoplot_options(show_data_points=False))
    .text_replace("United States", "USA", locations=loc.body(columns="country_name"))
    .data_color(columns="change", palette=["#FFF0FA", "#F900C3"])
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(weight="bold"),
        locations=[loc.body(columns="country_name"), loc.row_groups()],
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        "Midyear estimates.",
        locations=loc.spanner_labels(ids=["Population"]),
    )
    .opt_align_table_header(align="left")
)
```

Interact

Change [GT](./reference/GT.md#great_tables.GT) to [GTI](./reference/GTI.md#great_tables.GTI), and readers can sort, search and filter the table, with every format and style kept. Try sorting by a column, or filtering by the change.

``` python
(
    GTI(countries, groupname_col="region")
    .tab_header(
        title="The world's most populous countries",
        subtitle="And how they've grown since 1960",
    )
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"])
    .cols_label(
        country_code_2="",
        country_name="Country",
        pop_1960="1960",
        pop_2022="2022",
        change="Change",
        trend="1960-2020",
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
    .fmt_flag(columns="country_code_2")
    .fmt_number(columns=["pop_1960", "pop_2022"], compact=True, n_sigfig=3)
    .fmt_percent(columns="change", decimals=0, force_sign=True)
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", options=nanoplot_options(show_data_points=False))
    .text_replace("United States", "USA", locations=loc.body(columns="country_name"))
    .data_color(columns="change", palette=["#FFF0FA", "#F900C3"])
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(weight="bold"),
        locations=[loc.body(columns="country_name"), loc.row_groups()],
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        "Midyear estimates.",
        locations=loc.spanner_labels(ids=["Population"]),
    )
    .opt_align_table_header(align="left")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="change")
    .i_cols_controls(columns="country_code_2", sortable=False)
    .i_pagination(False)
    .i_responsive("scroll")
    .i_view(sort="-change")
)
```

### Format every kind of value

The `fmt_*()` methods format a table's values as numbers, currencies, percentages, dates and times, durations, units, chemical formulas, flags, icons, images and more, in any of hundreds of locales. The values themselves are kept: formatting only changes how they're shown. Where formats leave off, `sub_*()` methods put text in place of missing, zero, small or large values, and `text_*()` methods transform the text that formatting made.

``` python
import pandas as pd

examples = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ("Numbers", "fmt_number(compact=True)", 2_418_000_000),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_currency(currency=\"EUR\", locale=\"de\")", 1234.5),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_percent(decimals=1)", 0.4567),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_fraction()", 0.875),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_roman()", 2026),
        ("Numbers", "fmt_bytes()", 1_500_000_000),
        ("Dates and times", "fmt_date(date_style=\"wday_month_day_year\")", "2026-11-21"),
        ("Dates and times", "fmt_datetime(format_str=\"EEEE d MMMM\", locale=\"fr\")", "2026-11-21"),
        ("Dates and times", "fmt_duration(input_units=\"seconds\")", 3725),
        ("Science", "fmt_scientific()", 6.02214076e23),
        ("Science", "fmt_units()", "m s^-2"),
        ("Science", "fmt_chem()", "C6H12O6"),
        ("Symbols", "fmt_flag()", "JP"),
        ("Symbols", "fmt_icon()", "star"),
        ("Symbols", "fmt_tf(tf_style=\"check-mark\")", True),
    ],
    columns=["kind", "method", "shown"],
).assign(value=lambda df: df["shown"].map(repr))

(
    GT(examples[["kind", "method", "value", "shown"]], rowname_col="method", groupname_col="kind")
    .cols_label(value="Value", shown="Shown as")
    .fmt_number(columns="shown", rows=0, compact=True)
    .fmt_currency(columns="shown", rows=1, currency="EUR", locale="de")
    .fmt_percent(columns="shown", rows=2, decimals=1)
    .fmt_fraction(columns="shown", rows=3)
    .fmt_roman(columns="shown", rows=4)
    .fmt_bytes(columns="shown", rows=5)
    .fmt_date(columns="shown", rows=6, date_style="wday_month_day_year")
    .fmt_datetime(columns="shown", rows=7, format_str="EEEE d MMMM", locale="fr")
    .fmt_duration(columns="shown", rows=8, input_units="seconds")
    .fmt_scientific(columns="shown", rows=9)
    .fmt_units(columns="shown", rows=10)
    .fmt_chem(columns="shown", rows=11)
    .fmt_flag(columns="shown", rows=12)
    .fmt_icon(columns="shown", rows=13)
    .fmt_tf(columns="shown", rows=14, tf_style="check-mark")
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(font="ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace", size="0.85em"),
        locations=[loc.stub(), loc.body(columns="value")],
    )
    .tab_style(style=style.text(weight="bold"), locations=loc.body(columns="shown"))
    .tab_options(data_row_padding="5px", row_group_padding="6px")
)
```

| Numbers |  |  |
| fmt_number(compact=True) | 2418000000 | 2.42B |

### Let readers explore the data

A [GTI](./reference/GTI.md#great_tables.GTI) table is a [GT](./reference/GT.md#great_tables.GT) table that readers work with. Give its columns filters and small plots of their values, and it becomes a way to look through thousands of rows: all of it in the page, with no server. Here are the 1,851 films in competition at the Cannes Film Festival from 1946 to 2024. Pick a view below, or use the table's own controls, and the profiles under the column labels show what's left.

Ken Loach's films

The 1960s, longest first

From Japan, newest first

Under 90 minutes

Longest of each decade

Reset

``` python
films = (
    data.pl.films
    .with_columns(
        minutes=(
            pl.col("run_time").str.extract(r"(\d+)h").cast(pl.Int64).fill_null(0) * 60
            + pl.col("run_time").str.extract(r"(\d+)m").cast(pl.Int64).fill_null(0)
        ),
        decade=(pl.col("year") // 10 * 10).cast(pl.String) + "s",
        countries=pl.col("countries_of_origin").str.replace_all(",", ", "),
    )
    .select("year", "title", "director", "countries", "minutes", "decade")
)

(
    GTI(films, id="cannes")
    .tab_header(title="Films in competition at Cannes, 1946-2024")
    .cols_label(
        year="Year", title="Film", director="Director", countries="Countries",
        minutes="Length", decade="Decade",
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns="year", use_seps=False)
    .fmt_integer(columns="minutes", pattern="{x} min")
    .i_cols_filter(columns=["director", "countries"], type="text")
    .i_cols_filter(columns=["year", "minutes"])
    .i_cols_profile(columns=["year", "minutes"])
    .i_cols_controls(columns="decade", groupable=True, hideable=True)
    .i_export(["csv", "clipboard", "code"], filename="cannes")
    .i_pagination(page_size=8)
)
```

The code for the rows you see

Polars

Pandas

``` gth-livecode-code
```

Every view is a query that readers can edit as text (from the `{ }` button), and that `i_export("code")` turns into the Polars or Pandas code that gets the same rows from the data. Tables can start with a view of their own, keep the reader's view in the page's URL, open rows to show their details, link to each other, and fit narrow screens. In Shiny, Streamlit, Panel, Solara, marimo and notebooks, Python can read and set what readers do.

[Interactive tables with GTI →](./user-guide/gti-tables.md) [GTI in Python and apps →](./user-guide/gti-in-python-and-apps.md)

### Everything a table needs

##### Structure

Headers, footers, a stub of row labels, row groups, column spanners, footnotes and summary rows.

[The parts of a table →](./user-guide/header-footer-stub.md)

##### Style

Style any cell or part of a table, color cells by their values, and choose from premade themes and fonts.

[Styling the table →](./user-guide/styling-the-table-body.md)

##### Nanoplots

Small line, bar and box plots in the cells of a table, made from each row's values.

[Nanoplots →](./user-guide/nanoplots.md)

##### Any DataFrame

Polars, Pandas and PyArrow tables, and for [GTI](./reference/GTI.md#great_tables.GTI) tables, Polars LazyFrames, DuckDB relations and Ibis tables too.

[The datasets →](./user-guide/datasets.md)

##### Notebooks and apps

Tables show themselves in Jupyter, Quarto, marimo and VS Code, and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara apps.

[GTI in Python and apps →](./user-guide/gti-in-python-and-apps.md)

##### Export

HTML and LaTeX, images and PDFs, and with gridwell, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, RTF, Typst and SVG.

[Exporting and saving →](./user-guide/exporting-and-saving.md)

### Get started

Install Great Tables from PyPI:

``` bash
pip install great_tables
```

Then head over to the [User Guide](./user-guide/introduction.md) to make your first table, or look through the [Examples](./examples/) for ideas.
